identification.summary: Iran-origin cyber-espionage actor that Microsoft tracks as Hazel Sandstorm and maps to OilRig, APT34, EUROPIUM, HELIX KITTEN, COBALT GYPSY and Crambus [S1]. MITRE describes OilRig as a suspected Iranian group that has targeted Middle Eastern and international victims since at least 2014 in the financial, government, energy, chemical and telecommunications sectors. MITRE also says the group appears to carry out supply-chain attacks through trusted relationships [S2]. Mandiant (then FireEye) describes APT34 as a long-term espionage operation focused on reconnaissance that benefits Iranian nation-state interests [S3]. Reporting from 2021 to 2024 shows continued tool development and activity against Israel, Middle Eastern governments and Gulf targets [S6][S7][S8][S9].
identification.firstObserved: Mandiant/FireEye and MITRE: active since at least 2014 [S2][S3]. The first public OilRig campaign report (Unit 42) dates to May 2016 [S12].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Hazel Sandstorm (formerly EUROPIUM) [S1][S2]. MITRE tracks the actor as OilRig (G0049), which lists Hazel Sandstorm, EUROPIUM, APT34, Helix Kitten, COBALT GYPSY, IRN2, ITG13, Evasive Serpens, Earth Simnavaz, Crambus and TA452 as associated names [S2]. MITRE says APT34 and OilRig were once tracked as two groups and later combined [S2]. Mandiant says APT34 'loosely aligns' with OilRig and with elements of Greenbug [S3][S4]. CLUSTER WARNING: this record carries MITRE id G0003, which is MITRE's 'Cleaver' group (Operation Cleaver / TG-2889), a separate cluster [S2]. Microsoft's mapping does not list Cleaver, TG-2889, Tarh Andishan or Alibaba for Hazel Sandstorm [S1]. The record's imported aliases and software (TinyZBot, Net Crawler) come from that Cleaver cluster and should be reviewed. ESET files BladedFeline under its OilRig IOC set [S13]; this encyclopedia keeps a separate BladedFeline record.

attribution.sponsor: Iran. Mandiant/FireEye assesses that APT34 works on behalf of the Iranian government [S3]. In 2024 Mandiant described APT34 as a MOIS-affiliated group (Ministry of Intelligence and Security) [S5]. Microsoft lists Iran as the origin [S1].
attribution.confidence: Mandiant/FireEye: 'suspected Iranian' group assessed to work on behalf of the Iranian government [S3]. MITRE: 'suspected Iranian threat group' [S2]. Microsoft: origin Iran [S1]. No US government attribution of this cluster was found in the sources gathered. Vendor assessments are not government attribution.
attribution.basis: Mandiant/FireEye cites infrastructure details that contain references to Iran, use of Iranian infrastructure, and targeting that aligns with nation-state interests [S3]. MITRE repeats that basis [S2].

objectives: Long-term espionage and reconnaissance that benefits Iranian nation-state interests [S3]. Mandiant says the group collects strategic information about geopolitical and economic needs, and that its strongest interest is access to financial, energy and government entities [S4]. MITRE credits OilRig with collaborating on the destructive part of the 2019 ZeroCleare wiper attack on the Middle East energy sector, so the actor has at least supported disruptive operations [S2][S10].

regions: Iraq (recent operational pivot reported by Mandiant) [S5]
targeting.notes: Mandiant reports that in 2019-2020 organizations compromised by suspected APT34 actors had been compromised by UNC1860 before, or were compromised by it afterward. This suggests UNC1860 may give APT34 access or help it move laterally [S5]. MITRE says the group has used compromised organizations for supply-chain attacks on government entities [S2].

capabilities.summary: The group mainly uses spear phishing, often from compromised accounts, with social engineering [S3]. In 2019 it ran LinkedIn lures with a fake University of Cambridge persona and job-offer conversations [S4]. It has quickly weaponized Office exploits: it used CVE-2017-0199 in July 2017, and it used CVE-2017-11882 against a Middle Eastern government target less than a week after the patch [S3]. Its toolset is mostly custom PowerShell and .NET. Examples are POWRUNER and BONDUPDATER, which used a DGA and DNS-based C2 [S3]; TONEDEAF, VALUEVAULT, LONGWATCH and PICKPOCKET for credential theft and keylogging [S4]; and SideTwist [S11]. The ESET-reported downloaders are Solar, Mango, SampleCheck5000, OilCheck, ODAgent and OilBooster. Several of them use legitimate cloud and email services for C2 [S6][S7][S2]. PowerExchange is an Exchange-based PowerShell backdoor [S8]. MITRE also records IIS backdoors (RGDoor), web shells, Plink tunnels, Mimikatz and RMM tools such as ngrok [S2]. In 2024 Trend Micro reported exploitation of CVE-2024-30088 (Windows kernel elevation of privilege), password-filter DLL abuse, and exfiltration through Exchange [S9][S2].

campaigns.name: OilRig campaign (Helminth)
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 reports attacks on Saudi Arabian organizations that delivered the Helminth backdoor through macro-enabled Excel files.

campaigns.name: POWRUNER/BONDUPDATER via CVE-2017-0199
campaigns.summary: FireEye observes APT34 targeting a Middle Eastern organization with a malicious RTF file that exploited CVE-2017-0199.

campaigns.name: CVE-2017-11882 attack on Middle East government
campaigns.summary: Less than a week after the patch, APT34 uses the Office Equation Editor exploit against a Middle Eastern government organization to deploy POWRUNER and BONDUPDATER.

campaigns.name: LinkedIn 'Cambridge' phishing (TONEDEAF)
campaigns.summary: A fake University of Cambridge researcher on LinkedIn delivers TONEDEAF, VALUEVAULT and LONGWATCH to energy, utilities, government and oil and gas targets.

campaigns.name: ZeroCleare destructive attack
campaigns.summary: IBM reports a ZeroCleare wiper attack on the Middle East energy sector. MITRE records that OilRig collaborated on the destructive portion.

campaigns.name: SideTwist campaign
campaigns.summary: Check Point reports APT34 returning with an updated arsenal, including the SideTwist backdoor delivered by macro documents.

campaigns.name: Outer Space
campaigns.summary: Campaign against Israeli organizations using the SampleCheck5000 downloader and the Solar backdoor.

campaigns.name: Juicy Mix
campaigns.summary: Campaign against Israeli organizations using the Mango backdoor, the successor to Solar.

campaigns.name: Cloud-service-powered downloaders
campaigns.summary: ESET reports the SC5k, OilCheck, ODAgent and OilBooster downloaders, used since 2022 against Israeli organizations. They rely on legitimate cloud and email services.

campaigns.name: Crambus Middle Eastern government intrusion
campaigns.summary: Symantec reports a campaign against a Middle Eastern government that used the PowerExchange backdoor, Plink tunnels and Mimikatz.

campaigns.name: Earth Simnavaz attacks on Middle East
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro reports CVE-2024-30088 exploitation, password-filter DLLs, ngrok and exfiltration through Exchange against Middle Eastern targets.

diamond.adversary: Iran-origin operators that Microsoft tracks as Hazel Sandstorm [S1]. Mandiant assesses they work for the Iranian government and calls them MOIS-affiliated [S3][S5].
diamond.capability: Spear phishing and social-media lures; rapid Office exploit use (CVE-2017-0199, CVE-2017-11882); custom PowerShell and .NET backdoors and downloaders; IIS and Exchange backdoors; credential theft; and CVE-2024-30088 privilege escalation [S2][S3][S4][S8][S9].
diamond.infrastructure: Actor-registered look-alike domains such as cam-research-ac[.]com and offlineearthquake[.]com [S4]; DGA subdomains and DNS-based C2 [S3]; legitimate cloud and email services used for C2 [S7]; compromised Exchange servers used for exfiltration [S9][S2]; and compromised third-party organizations [S2].
diamond.victim: Middle Eastern government, financial, energy, chemical and telecommunications organizations; Israeli organizations; and IT providers used as supply-chain access [S2][S3][S6][S7].
diamond.socioPolitical: Strategic intelligence for Iran's economic and national-security goals, with tempo expected to rise during regional geopolitical tension [S4].
diamond.technology: Microsoft Office and Windows endpoints, on-premises Exchange and IIS servers, and trust in professional networks such as LinkedIn [S3][S4][S8][S9].

gaps: Microsoft's own Hazel Sandstorm reporting (Microsoft Security blog) could not be opened because microsoft.com returned 403. Only Microsoft's public naming feed was used [S1].

Several primary reports were cited only through MITRE ATT&CK's dated references and procedure text, because the hosts were unreachable: ESET (welivesecurity.com), Symantec (security.com), Trend Micro, IBM X-Force, Check Point and Unit 42 [S6][S7][S8][S9][S10][S11][S12]. The details of those reports have not been checked against the originals.
Web search was unavailable during this research pass (session search budget exhausted), so 2025-2026 activity is not covered.

The record's MITRE id G0003 (Cleaver) does not match. MITRE maps Hazel Sandstorm to OilRig G0049 [S2]. The imported Cleaver, Operation Cleaver, TG-2889, Tarh Andishan and Alibaba aliases, and the TinyZBot and Net Crawler software, belong to the Cleaver cluster and need review.
Government attribution: no US or allied government statement that names this cluster was found in the sources gathered. Mandiant's MOIS affiliation is a vendor assessment [S5].
The boundaries with Greenbug, Lyceum, UNC1860 and BladedFeline are unclear. Vendors describe overlap or cooperation, not identity [S4][S5][S13].
OilRig's exact role in ZeroCleare ('collaborated on the destructive portion') rests on MITRE's summary of IBM reporting and was not checked against the original [S2][S10].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key terrain includes partner-nation government, energy and telecom networks in the Middle East; on-premises Exchange and IIS servers; and IT service providers with trusted access [S2][S8][S9]. STEP 2 (effects): Fast exploit uptake (days after a patch) and C2 that blends into DNS and legitimate cloud and email traffic shorten detection windows and weaken perimeter controls [S3][S7]. STEP 3 (adversary template): The usual chain is a social-engineering or spear-phishing lure (including LinkedIn job or academic personas), then a PowerShell or .NET backdoor, then credential theft (Mimikatz, VALUEVAULT, password filters), then Plink/RDP tunneling, then exfiltration through Exchange or cloud services [S2][S4][S8][S9]. STEP 4: MLCOA is persistent espionage against Gulf and Israeli government and energy targets through mail-server backdoors. Candidate indicators: anomalous Exchange mailbox drafts or rules, new password-filter DLLs, ngrok or Plink binaries renamed under ProgramData, and scheduled tasks running VBS or PowerShell every minute [S2][S3][S9]. MDCOA is handing access to a destructive operation (wiper) against energy-sector partners, as in ZeroCleare [S2][S10]; candidate indicator: RawDisk driver loading.
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track Hazel Sandstorm, OilRig, APT34, Crambus and Earth Simnavaz reporting together under one entry, and flag the separate Cleaver, UNC1860 and BladedFeline clusters [S1][S2][S5]. Authorities: activity against partner-nation networks and third-party IT providers needs coordination with mission partners and host-nation authorities before defensive actions on non-DoD terrain [S2]. Mission assurance: prioritize hardening and monitoring of Exchange and IIS servers that support theater coordination with Gulf partners, and patch Office and Windows privilege-escalation CVEs quickly [S3][S8][S9]. Coordination: share indicators about LinkedIn and social-media lures with personnel security and OPSEC staff, because the actor targets individuals through professional networks [S4].
